sentences.text: The holotype specimen includes a skull, lower jaws, vertebrae, a left ulna and hand, and parts of the legs and pubis.
The type specimen is a juvenile measuring about 1 meter long and weighing approximately 1.5 kilograms, representing a small bipedal predator.
The skull contains a nearly complete scleral ring made of overlapping ossicles in the right eye socket, a structure composed of overlapping bonelets.
The hand claws are distinct, with a large curved thumb claw and two smaller claws with straight undersides.
In the depression of the cranial opening, the antorbital fenestra, there is a second opening in front, the maxillary fenestra, which occupies most of this depression.
Teeth in the maxilla had denticles only on their posterior edges, which are very small and point toward the tips of the teeth.
Aorun is the oldest known coelurosaur from the Shishugou Formation and the seventh theropod found there.
The fossil preserves an almost complete scleral ring in the eye socket, offering rare insight into the visual system of early theropods.
Histological analysis suggests the holotype specimen was at most one year old and was not a perinate.
Researchers initially found an exposed leg bone on the surface before digging up the skull underneath.
The species Aorun zhaoi was named and described in 2013 by Choiniere, Clark, Forster, Norell, Eberth, Erickson, Hongjun, and Xu.

The holotype specimen of Aorun zhaoi (IVPP V15709) was recovered from the Wucaiwan locality in the lower half of the Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin, Xinjiang, China, from reddish-brown terrestrial mudstone dated to approximately 161.2 million years ago.
The genus name Aorun is derived from the Chinese mythical deity Ao Run, the Dragon King of the West Sea, and is the abbreviated masculine name of Ao Run in Mandarin Chinese.
Aorun was likely a predator of small lizards and mammals.
Cervical vertebrae are moderately opisthocoelous: with centers convex in the front and concave in the back.
The tibia has only a high and narrow groove on its front outer side that functioned as contact with the top of the astragalus, although this ascending process is low.
The original authors classified Aorun as a basal member of Coelurosauria and a member of Coeluridae.
Aorun is classified within the unranked group Coelurosauria.
Authors placed Aorun in a basal position within Coelurosauria, but in any case it is more derived than Tyrannosauroidea.
It is possible that Aorun is a member of Coeluridae, which is the most basal clade of Maniraptora.
The parent group listed for Aorun in the Paleobiology Database is Alvarezsauria.
Aorun is distinct from other theropods found in the same region, including Guanlong, Haplocheirus, Limusaurus, Monolophosaurus, Sinraptor, and Zuolong.

Radiometric dating places the fossil deposits at approximately 161.6 million years old, at the boundary of the Oxfordian and Callovian stages, while the time range for Aorun is the Callovian stage, from 165.3 to 161.5 million years ago.
The paleoenvironment was warm but experienced a basin-wide seasonal dry climate, and the paleoecosystem of the Shishugou Formation was warm and humid but had a dry season across the basin.
Some researchers debate whether Aorun should be classified as a carnosaurian rather than a coelurosaurian.
Researchers note that coding immature taxa as adults can artificially place them in basal positions in phylogenetic analyses.
Some analyses suggest Aorun may be a basal alvarezsaur, a classification that has been questioned by other researchers.
A 2024 analysis by Cau recovered Aorun as a basal member of the superfamily Allosauroidea.
